The nine-banded armadillo, Dasypus novemcinctus, is a medium-sized xenarthran whose total length from the tip of the snout to the end of the tail can reach approximately 90 centimeters [Li = approximately 90 centimeters]. Field measurements across its extensive range, which stretches from the southern United States through Central America into northern Argentina, indicate that adult individuals commonly attain a head-body length of 64 to 107 centimeters [Li = 64 to 107 centimeters], with the tail accounting for roughly forty percent of the overall body length. The species is noted for its distinctive bony carapace, which is composed of a shield over the shoulders, a series of movable bands across the midsection, and a rear pelvic shield. This armor provides substantial protection against predators, although the armadillo relies more heavily on its ability to burrow rapidly in response to threats. The body mass of a fully grown adult is typically reported as approximately 5,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 5,500 grams], though particularly large specimens from well-resourced habitats have been documented at up to 10 kilograms [Wwi = up to 10 kilograms], highlighting considerable intraspecific variation linked to local environmental conditions and prey abundance.

Reproduction in Dasypus novemcinctus is characterized by a remarkably consistent pattern of monozygotic polyembryony, in which a single fertilized egg divides to produce four genetically identical offspring. Females typically produce a single litter each year, and the maximum reproductive output, expressed as four pups per litter [N_R_i = four pups per litter] with one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], is sustained under favorable thermal conditions. Within the range of the species' normal body temperature, estimated at 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C], this reproductive schedule represents a substantial annual investment in offspring production, constrained by the energetic demands of gestation and subsequent lactation. The birth of a litter of four pups, each weighing approximately 66 grams [Wwb = approximately 66 grams], underscores the considerable maternal allocation required to bring these precocial offspring to term. The newborn armadillos are fully formed and active, with their eyes open, though they remain entirely dependent on the female for several weeks while they nurse and develop the capacity to forage independently.

Gestation in the nine-banded armadillo is notably extended, a consequence of a facultative embryonic diapause period during which the blastocyst remains unimplanted for several months. Under the typical thermal regime of the species, with a core body temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C], the total duration from fertilization to parturition spans approximately 133 days [tg = approximately 133 days]. This extended period encompasses both the delayed implantation phase and the subsequent active gestation, during which the four embryos develop within the uterine lining. Following the birth of the pups, the pre-weaning interval represents another critical life-history stage, as the young remain in the burrow nursing from the mother. The time since birth at weaning is roughly 137 days [tx = roughly 137 days] at a body temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C], a period during which the pups transition from a milk-based diet to consuming solid foods, primarily insects, grubs, and other invertebrates. This developmental trajectory reflects the species' slow pace of early growth relative to its overall reproductive output.

The pace of maturation in Dasypus novemcinctus is relatively slow for a mammal of its body size, reflecting the allocation of resources toward the growth of the bony carapace and the maintenance of a low metabolic rate characteristic of xenarthrans. Sexual maturity, or the time since birth at puberty, is attained at around 365 days [tp = around 365 days] at a body temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C], meaning that individuals born in the spring of one year are capable of reproducing by the same season of the following year. This age at first potential reproduction is delayed relative to many similarly-sized placental mammals, a phenomenon linked to the armadillo's limited capacity for rapid energy acquisition and its substantial investment in structural defenses. Once mature, the female armadillo can enter into an annual reproductive cycle that includes the embryonic diapause mechanism. This life history strategy, which balances a moderate birth mass against an extended developmental schedule, has proven highly successful across the species' broad geographic distribution.

Longevity in the nine-banded armadillo is moderate among xenarthrans, with the maximum lifespan documented for individuals at a typical core body temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C] reaching approximately 22.3 years [am = approximately 22.3 years]. This figure, derived from records of wild and captive specimens, places the species at the upper end of the longevity range for medium-sized burrowing mammals, exceeding expectations based solely on body mass. Field studies have noted that adult mortality is heavily influenced by predation from large carnivores, vehicle strikes, and extreme weather events, rather than by intrinsic senescence. The species' relatively long life permits multiple reproductive seasons, thereby compensating for its modest litter production of just one event per year. This extended reproductive window, combined with the guaranteed production of four offspring per event, ensures that a single female can contribute substantially to population recruitment over her lifetime, reinforcing the armadillo's status as a highly successful and resilient inhabitant of Neotropical and subtropical ecosystems.
